werk/carole-king-fantasy.text:
Fantasy was released in 1973 as Carole King's fifth album. It is conceived as a kind of song cycle: it opens and closes with two versions of the title track, and on each side the songs run straight into one another. It climbed to number six on the Billboard 200 and has been held in high regard by her fans for decades.

The sound is broad. Alongside King on piano, the musicians include guitarist David T. Walker, bassist Charles Larkey, drummer Harvey Mason, saxophonists, trumpeters, trombonists and a string section. Eddie Kendricks sings backing vocals. King wrote the string and horn arrangements herself. Corazón, a Spanish-language song with a Latin flavour, became a modest hit. So did Believe In Humanity, which the AllMusic reviewer called the best song on the album. The B-side You Light Up My Life charted separately.
werk/carole-king-fantasy.listen: Listen to the rhythm in Corazón: the Latin flavour and the Spanish make this song stand apart from the rest of the album.

werk/carole-king-music.text:
Music is Carole King's third studio album. It was released in December 1971 and continues the style of Tapestry. The record was produced by Lou Adler. The songs are all her own, and on many tracks she plays piano and celeste. The photograph on the cover was taken at 8815 Appian Way in Laurel Canyon, California.

The album includes Brother, Brother, It's Going to Take Some Time and Sweet Seasons. The former became a hit for the Carpenters, while the latter reached number 9 in the United States under its own steam. Horn players such as saxophonist Curtis Amy and flautist and reed player Plas Johnson join in. The album was an instant success, went gold in December and was at number 1 on New Year's Day 1972. It was less groundbreaking than Tapestry, but it meant that both records were in the top ten at the same time.
werk/carole-king-music.listen: Listen to Sweet Seasons and notice the horns, including Curtis Amy on tenor saxophone, alongside the piano.

werk/carole-king-rhymes-en-reasons.text:
Rhymes & Reasons is the first commercial studio album by the American singer and songwriter John Denver and was released in October 1969 on RCA Records. In 2005 it was reissued on CD by Legacy Recordings.

The best-known song has a long history. Denver wrote Leaving on a Jet Plane in 1966 and recorded it under the title Babe I Hate to Go on his first demo record, John Denver Sings. Producer Milt Okun persuaded him to change the title. After Peter, Paul and Mary had a hit with it in 1969, he recorded the song again for this album and released it as a single. It did not chart. In 1973 he recorded it for the third and last time.
werk/carole-king-rhymes-en-reasons.listen: Listen to Leaving on a Jet Plane, a song he had already written in 1966; this is his second recording of it.

werk/carole-king-tapestry.text:
Carole King had been writing hits since the early 1960s, often with her then husband Gerry Goffin, but mainly for other singers. James Taylor encouraged her to sing her own songs. Tapestry, her second studio album, was recorded in January 1971 in Studio B at A&M in Los Angeles. The producer was Lou Adler; Taylor, Joni Mitchell and experienced session musicians supported her. The album was released on 10 February 1971.

She wrote all the songs herself or with others. Goffin co-wrote the lyrics of, among others, Will You Love Me Tomorrow and (You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman, which had already been hits for The Shirelles and Aretha Franklin. The single It's Too Late, with I Feel the Earth Move, spent five weeks at number one. A Rolling Stone reviewer praised its remarkable personal intimacy. The album won four Grammys, including Album of the Year.
werk/carole-king-tapestry.listen: Listen to how close and personal the vocal sounds in It's Too Late, as if there were only one listener.

werk/carole-king-writer.text:
Writer is Carole King's debut album and was released in May 1970. By then she already had a successful career as a songwriter behind her and had formed the short-lived group The City in Los Angeles. The album was recorded at Crystal Sound in Hollywood and produced by John Fischbach, the studio's co-founder. Gerry Goffin mixed it, and James Taylor plays acoustic guitar.

The album includes her own versions of Up on the Roof, a hit for the Drifters in 1962, and of Child of Mine, a song recorded by Billy Joe Royal, among others. On release the record attracted little attention. Only after the success of Tapestry in 1971 did Writer enter the charts. Critics were positive: AllMusic called it the most underrated of her original albums. In Rolling Stone, Jon Landau found the production weak, but thought the album worth hearing despite its flaws.
werk/carole-king-writer.listen: Listen to Up On the Roof, a song that had earlier been a hit for the Drifters, and notice how it sounds here as a songwriter's version, with the piano and the voice up front.

werk/carpenters-a-song-for-you.text:
A Song for You, released in June 1972, was the fourth studio album by the American duo Carpenters. Richard Carpenter intended it as a kind of concept album: the title song by Leon Russell opens and closes the record, and the songs in between together make up the song. Six tracks were released as singles. Hurting Each Other, a cover of the Ruby & the Romantics song, reached number two. Goodbye to Love featured a fuzz guitar solo by Tony Peluso, which startled some radio stations, and it had a great influence on later power ballads.

Top of the World, the biggest hit and later a number one, was not released until well over a year after the album, because Richard had underestimated its appeal. Billboard praised Jack Daugherty's production and the musical quality. Bruce Eder of AllMusic called the album the duo's best and the high point of their recording career.
werk/carpenters-a-song-for-you.listen: Listen to Goodbye to Love and wait for Tony Peluso's fuzz guitar solo, a sound some radio stations saw nothing in.

werk/carpenters-carpenters.text:
This third album by the duo was released on 14 May 1971 and became their most successful studio album. It reached number two on the US Billboard 200 and number twelve in the United Kingdom. The original sleeve, with an overlapping flap, looked like a large brown envelope. For that reason fans call the record the Tan Album, a nod to the Beatles' White Album. Outside North America the cover usually showed a photograph of the duo.

The hits are For All We Know, Rainy Days and Mondays and Superstar. Rainy Days and Mondays, written by Roger Nichols and Paul Williams, reached number two on the US Hot 100. Almost all the lead vocals are Karen's. Richard sings lead on Druscilla Penny, on Saturday and on part of the Bacharach and David medley. According to the source, the strength of these recordings convinced Richard to put his sister at the front live instead of behind the drums. The album earned four Grammy nominations.
werk/carpenters-carpenters.listen: Listen to Saturday, which lasts only 1:18, and notice who is singing lead: here it is Richard, with Karen in the background.

werk/carpenters-close-to-you.text:
Close to You was released on 19 August 1970 and was the second album by the American duo Carpenters. The first album, Offering, had received little attention. This time it caught on: the record reached number two on the US album chart and topped the chart in Canada. Two singles were responsible. (They Long To Be) Close To You was the first Burt Bacharach and Hal David composition the duo recorded, and it stayed at number one for four weeks. We've Only Just Begun began as music for a bank commercial.

The record also includes covers, such as Help by Lennon and McCartney and Reason To Believe by Tim Hardin. Mr. Guder is dedicated to the boss who fired Richard and lyricist John Bettis at Disneyland because they kept on playing modern songs. The album earned eight Grammy nominations, including one for Album of the Year. The duo won the award for Best New Artist.
werk/carpenters-close-to-you.listen: Listen to Maybe It's You and notice the oboe in the arrangement. That solo is played by Doug Strawn.

werk/carpenters-now-en-then.text:
Now & Then, the Carpenters' fifth studio album, was released on 1 May 1973. The title was an idea of their mother Agnes and comes from a song that did not make it onto the record. Because 1973 saw a revival of old hits, the second side is a medley of oldies, beginning with their own song Yesterday Once More. Guitarist Tony Peluso can be heard in it as a radio DJ, with, among others, The End of the World, Dead Man's Curve, Johnny Angel and One Fine Day.

The first side opens with Sing, written by Joe Raposo of Sesame Street. The record company did not want it as a single, but Richard insisted. He wrote Yesterday Once More after hearing the melody in his head while driving. The provisional chorus lyrics stayed, and the song became the duo's biggest worldwide hit. Rolling Stone praised the second side in particular, and Billboard called the idea of the radio show unique.
werk/carpenters-now-en-then.listen: Listen to Yesterday Once More and notice the chorus, which kept its provisional lyrics, sha-la-la-wo-wo-wo.

werk/cassandra-wilson-dance-to-the-drums.text:
This is the seventh studio album by the American jazz singer Cassandra Wilson. It was released in 1992 on Columbia. She produced it herself, together with guitarist Jean-Paul Bourelly, with whom she also wrote most of the songs. Pianist James Weidman and bassist Kevin Bruce Harris play on several tracks, alongside various drummers and percussionists. On Amazing Grace she sings a well-known song by John Newton, accompanying herself on piano.

Scott Yanow wrote in AllMusic that with this record Wilson was at a crossroads in her career. A reviewer for New York magazine thought the album benefits greatly from the strength of its material, which comes largely from Wilson and Bourelly.
werk/cassandra-wilson-dance-to-the-drums.listen: Listen to Amazing Grace: notice the piano part Wilson plays herself and how she sings the familiar song.

werk/cassandra-wilson-new-moon-daughter.text:
New Moon Daughter was released in 1995 on Blue Note and followed Blue Light 'til Dawn. Wilson named the album after an old Ashanti proverb: sickness comes with the waning moon, the new moon heals. It contains twelve tracks, five of them her own. She also sings Strange Fruit by Billie Holiday, Love Is Blindness by U2 and Last Train to Clarksville by the Monkees.

The press responded very positively. Critics thought the album at least as good as its predecessor. They praised her deep, dark contralto and her long, mesmerizing phrasing. Rolling Stone found it more sensitive and darker than Blue Light 'til Dawn. There were also critical voices, among other things about the slow tempo. The album reached number 1 on Billboard's jazz chart and won a Grammy for Best Jazz Vocal Performance.
werk/cassandra-wilson-new-moon-daughter.listen: Listen to Love Is Blindness and notice how a pop song by U2 takes on a slow, dark atmosphere in her hands.

werk/cassandra-wilson-rendezvous.text:
Rendezvous is a duo album by singer Cassandra Wilson and pianist Jacky Terrasson, released on 23 September 1997 by Blue Note. The title comes from a ballad by Herbie Hancock. It was recorded in January and April 1997 at Clinton Recording Studios in New York. Terrasson wrote all the arrangements. The album was recorded and mixed in analogue, without noise reduction and without equalizers in mastering.

The programme consists mainly of jazz and pop standards, with one song by Terrasson. With only piano, bass and percussion, the voice sounds barer than on her earlier records. One reviewer heard in Wilson a more vulnerable Nina Simone. The mood is dark and thoughtful. The reviews were mostly glowing, but The New York Times called it a mediocre standards album.
werk/cassandra-wilson-rendezvous.listen: Listen to Autumn Leaves and notice how the piano leaves room for the voice and how softly Wilson lets the syllables trail off.

werk/cassius-1999.text:
This double album was released on 27 October 1982 on Warner Bros. It was the first record Prince made with his band the Revolution. It became his commercial breakthrough and his first album in the US top ten.

The sound revolves around synthesizers and drum machines, notably the Linn LM-1. The title song is a protest against nuclear weapons. Little Red Corvette brought Prince to a broader rock audience, and the rockabilly-like single Delirious reached the US top ten. Automatic lasts almost ten minutes and opens the third side. Something in the Water (Does Not Compute) shows how strongly the computer age colours the record. Two ballads, Free and International Lover, provide moments of calm. The videos for 1999 and Little Red Corvette received heavy airplay on MTV, at a time when black artists were hardly seen there. The Rolling Stone Album Guide calls the record perhaps Prince's most influential album, because its arrangements defined the Minneapolis sound.
werk/cassius-1999.listen: Listen to Little Red Corvette and notice how the drum machine and synthesizers form the tight foundation on which the melody rests.

werk/cecil-taylor-the-world-of-cecil-tay.text:
This album was recorded in New York in October 1960 for the Candid label. Pianist Cecil Taylor plays on it with saxophonist Archie Shepp, bassist Buell Neidlinger and drummer Denis Charles. Some pieces are improvisations done in a single take, others were assembled from several takes. For the piece Air it took twenty-nine attempts before he was satisfied.

An AllMusic reviewer called it a wonderful document from the early part of his career, when he was caught between arrangements of standards and his own radical experiments. He also heard in it a deep feeling for the blues that always remained, however abstract the music became. DownBeat gave the album four stars and heard a spontaneous form of Third Stream, a blend of jazz and contemporary classical music.
werk/cecil-taylor-the-world-of-cecil-tay.listen: Listen to Air and notice the conversation between piano, bass and drums. Try to hear the feeling for the blues beneath the loose sounds all the same.

werk/cecil-taylor-unit-structures.text:
Unit Structures was released in October 1966 on Blue Note and was Cecil Taylor's first album for that label. Later that same year he recorded Conquistador! with a similar line-up, which did not come out until 1968. The record came with an essay by Taylor himself, about sound and structure.

The music is free jazz in a particularly intense form. A Pitchfork reviewer called it one of the most ferocious early free jazz albums and wrote that the atonality does not let up. Yet the group of seven players finds beautiful spaces. Free jazz here means not only improvising freely, but also devising your own musical worlds and rules. The album received five stars from AllMusic and in 2017 appeared on Pitchfork's list of the two hundred best albums of the 1960s.
werk/cecil-taylor-unit-structures.listen: Listen to Steps and notice how the players sound all through one another. Don't look for a melody, but for energy and colour.

werk/cecile-mclorin-salvant-dreams-and-d.text:
Dreams and Daggers was released on 29 September 2017 on Mack Avenue Records, as a set of two CDs or three LPs. Singer Cécile McLorin Salvant combines recordings from the Village Vanguard with studio recordings from the DiMenna Center for Classical Music. Pianist Aaron Diehl, bassist Paul Sikivie and drummer Lawrence Leathers accompany her, and the Catalyst Quartet plays the strings on six tracks. She co-produced and made the drawings and handwriting in the booklet herself.

The repertoire consists of standards and a few original songs, all about love and heartbreak. An AllMusic reviewer gave it five stars and Stereophile called it the best jazz vocal album in ten years. The album earned her a second Grammy, for Best Jazz Vocal Album, and a nomination for an NAACP Image Award.
werk/cecile-mclorin-salvant-dreams-and-d.listen: Listen to And Yet, one of the tracks with the Catalyst Quartet, and notice how the strings and her voice frame each other.

werk/celia-cruz-son-con-guaguanco.text:
Son con guaguancó was released in 1966 on Tico Records. It was Celia Cruz's first major solo record in the United States without the Sonora Matancera, the orchestra with which she had earlier made her breakthrough. Al Santiago produced the album. The arrangements were by Bobby Valentin, Charlie Palmieri, Louie Ramirez and Tito Puente. The band was known as the Alegre All Stars.

According to AllMusic the record sounds full of heat and energy, with perhaps the best salsa band ever assembled. The album did not sell as well as later Cruz records, but according to the magazine Songlines it became a decisive door to greater success. It is now regarded as one of the great works of Latin American music. In a 2024 list of the 600 best Latin American albums it stands at number 8, and in 2018 NPR included it in a list of the 150 best albums by women.
werk/celia-cruz-son-con-guaguanco.listen: Listen to Son con Guaguancó and notice the interplay between Cruz's voice and the band: how do the instruments respond to her voice?

werk/celine-dion-falling-into-you.text:
Falling Into You was released on 11 March 1996, after The Colour of My Love and the French-language D'eux. Dion wanted to broaden her sound and worked with fourteen producers, including Jim Steinman and David Foster. The album features elaborate orchestral arrangements, African-tinged vocals and instruments such as violin, Spanish guitar and saxophone. Three songs are English adaptations of songs from D'eux.

The key songs are Because You Loved Me, written by Diane Warren for the film Up Close and Personal, and It's All Coming Back to Me Now, a power ballad by Steinman. All By Myself and River Deep, Mountain High also received a version of their own. The album received glowing reviews and won both Album of the Year and Best Pop Album at the 39th Grammy Awards. It became her best-selling record.
werk/celine-dion-falling-into-you.listen: Listen to It's All Coming Back to Me Now and notice the dramatic orchestration and the classical piano passages.

werk/celine-dion-incognito.text:
Incognito is the eighth French-language studio album by the Canadian singer Céline Dion and her first release on a major record label. CBS Records released it in Quebec on 2 April 1987. The album showed a new image, a more contemporary direction and a renewed group of writers and producers. Jean Roussel, Aldo Nova and Pierre Bazinet produced the eight tracks. Délivre-moi is a French-language adaptation of Love in the Shadows by E. G. Daily.

Six singles were released in Quebec, and all of them reached the top five of the airplay chart. Four of them became number one: Incognito, Lolita (Trop jeune pour aimer), Comme un cœur froid and D'abord, c'est quoi l'amour. The album went double platinum in Canada.
werk/celine-dion-incognito.listen: Listen to Incognito, the title song that spent six weeks at number one in Quebec, and notice how the singer's voice carries the song.

werk/celine-dion-the-colour-of-my-love.text:
The Colour of My Love is Céline Dion's twelfth studio album and her third in English. It was recorded in Los Angeles from June to September 1993 and released in November 1993. David Foster, Ric Wake, Walter Afanasieff, Christopher Neil and Guy Roche produced; Diane Warren wrote four songs. Before that, Dion had already had success with the duet Beauty and the Beast.

The result is a smooth mix of ballads and pop songs. The Power of Love, a cover of the Jennifer Rush song, became her first number one in the United States. Think Twice spent five weeks at the top in Great Britain. The album also includes When I Fall in Love, a duet with Clive Griffin for the film Sleepless in Seattle. The reviews were mostly positive, and the album became one of the best-selling ever. In 1995 it won two Juno Awards.
werk/celine-dion-the-colour-of-my-love.listen: Listen to When I Fall in Love and notice how her voice and Clive Griffin's sound together.

werk/celine-dion-unison.text:
Unison is Céline Dion's ninth studio album and her first in English. Columbia and Epic released it on 2 April 1990. CBS initially offered a modest budget of 25,000 dollars to put English vocals over existing tracks from Incognito. Thanks to the duet Can't We Try with Dan Hill, her performance of Have a Heart at the 1987 Juno Awards and David Foster's interest, the budget rose to 600,000 dollars. It was recorded in London, New York and Los Angeles.

The album combines dance pop and soft rock. Where Does My Heart Beat Now became her first major American hit and reached number four on the Billboard Hot 100. The reviews were mostly positive. At the 1991 Juno Awards Unison won the award for Album of the Year.
werk/celine-dion-unison.listen: Listen to Where Does My Heart Beat Now, her first major American hit, and notice how the vocal carries the song.

werk/chaka-khan-ask-rufus.text:
Ask Rufus is the fifth studio album by the funk band Rufus, released in 1977 on ABC Records. The recording was difficult because of tensions between Chaka Khan and drummer Andre Fischer, after she had married Richard Holland. As a result the recording took longer than for earlier albums. It was the last album with Fischer. Keyboardist David Hawk Wolinski joined the band, and former member Dennis Belfield returned to write Everlasting Love together with Wolinski and Kevin Murphy.

The album spent three weeks at the top of the R&B chart and reached number 14 on the pop chart. The singles were At Midnight (My Love Will Lift You Up), Hollywood and Everlasting Love. Billboard called it the work of a mature artist, while Robert Christgau was less impressed. Erykah Badu later covered Hollywood, and in 2020 Rolling Stone placed the record at number 499 on its list of the 500 greatest albums of all time.
werk/chaka-khan-ask-rufus.listen: Listen to At Midnight (My Love Will Lift You Up) and notice the horns underneath the vocal.

werk/chaka-khan-masterjam.text:
Masterjam is the eighth album by the funk band Rufus and the seventh with singer Chaka Khan. It was released in 1979 and was their first record on MCA, which had taken over the ABC label. The producer was Quincy Jones, with whom Khan had already worked a year earlier. He brought in the Seawind Horns and the Brothers Johnson, and the band even plays a funky version of his own Body Heat.

That year Khan also had solo success with I'm Every Woman, while she was still attached to the band. Tony Maiden sang more and more songs for Rufus. Do You Love What You Feel became the group's fourth number 1 on the R&B chart. Masterjam topped the R&B album chart and reached number 14 on the pop chart.
werk/chaka-khan-masterjam.listen: Listen to Body Heat, a song by Quincy Jones himself, and notice how the band turns it into a funky version.

werk/chaka-khan-rufusized.text:
Rufusized is the third studio album by the Chicago funk band Rufus and was released at the end of 1974 on ABC Records, already the second album of that year. Since 1972 Chaka Khan had been the singer, after Paulette McWilliams left. After the success of Rags to Rufus, the band's breakthrough, the group quickly went back into the studio to keep up the momentum. She now contributed more often as a writer, including on instrumental pieces. Bob Monaco produced.

The record reached number 2 on the R&B chart and number 7 on the pop chart and sold a million copies. Once You Get Started and Please Pardon Me were hits, and Somebody's Watching You, Pack'd My Bags and I'm a Woman are regarded as favourites on the album. I'm a Woman appeared four years before I'm Every Woman. The band ended 1974 as newcomers and began 1975 as headliners.
werk/chaka-khan-rufusized.listen: Listen to Once You Get Started, one of the hits, and notice the interplay between the singer and the band.

werk/charles-lloyd-nirvana.text:
Nirvana by saxophonist Charles Lloyd was mostly recorded in 1965, but Columbia did not release it until 1968. The record is therefore a collection of sessions from different years. Island Blues, Carcara, Long Time, Baby, Love Theme from In Harm's Way and Sun Dance come from October 1965, with Gábor Szabó on guitar, Albert Stinson on bass and Pete LaRoca on drums. East of the Sun and You Know are older, with Ron Carter and Tony Williams.

The closing piece One for Joan/Freedom Traveler lasts almost fifteen minutes and was recorded as early as 1962, with trombonist Garnett Brown and drummer Chico Hamilton. It had previously appeared on Hamilton's album Drumfusion. Love Theme from In Harm's Way was written by Jerry Goldsmith. On the record Lloyd plays tenor saxophone and flute.
werk/charles-lloyd-nirvana.listen: Listen to One for Joan/Freedom Traveler, the longest piece on the record, and notice how the music develops, with Prayer and Journey as parts in the title.

werk/charles-lloyd-of-course-of-course.text:
Of Course, Of Course was the second album saxophonist Charles Lloyd made for Columbia. He plays tenor saxophone and flute, together with guitarist Gábor Szabó, bassist Ron Carter and drummer Tony Williams. It was recorded in Columbia Studio A in New York, spread over three sessions: in May 1964 and in March and October 1965.

Lloyd wrote most of the music himself. In addition there are two older songs: The Best Thing for You by Irving Berlin and The Things We Did Last Summer by Sammy Cahn and Jule Styne. The reviewers Scott Yanow and Thom Jurek gave the record four stars. According to them, Lloyd showed here, on tenor and on flute, that he was quickly finding a voice of his own, and they called it an underrated album and a minor classic.
werk/charles-lloyd-of-course-of-course.listen: Listen to The Best Thing for You, a song by Irving Berlin, and notice how Lloyd gives it a voice of his own.

werk/charles-lloyd-waves.text:
Waves is a 1972 album by the jazz saxophonist Charles Lloyd. He plays tenor saxophone, flute and alto flute. He recorded it with jazz musicians such as guitarist Gábor Szabó and drummer Woodrow Theus, but also with rock musicians. Roger McGuinn of The Byrds plays twelve-string guitar, and Al Jardine, Carl Wilson and Mike Love of The Beach Boys sing along on the opening track TM.

It was recorded at Malibu Road. The result is a blend of jazz, fusion and hippie rock. The reception was mixed. AllMusic gave it two stars and found the music mainly soothing and rather faceless. Another reviewer saw it precisely as proof that a jazz musician could move smoothly into fusion and hippie rock, and that too few people know the album.
werk/charles-lloyd-waves.listen: Listen to TM and notice how saxophone, twelve-string guitar and backing vocals blend.

werk/charles-mingus-blues-en-roots.text:
Blues & Roots was recorded on 4 February 1959 at Atlantic Studios in New York and released in 1960 on Atlantic. A year earlier, producer Nesuhi Ertegun had proposed making a complete blues record in the style of Haitian Fight Song. Some critics thought Mingus did not swing enough. Ertegun wanted to serve them a stream of soul music: churchy, bluesy, swinging and earthy.

Mingus hesitated, because he also wanted to do other things than just swing. Even so, he agreed. He surrounded himself with a large ensemble, including four saxophonists and two trombonists. Dannie Richmond played drums. DownBeat called the record important music that is worth listening to carefully. Q Magazine praised how Mingus drove his fellow musicians on with his bass playing and hoarse shouts of encouragement.
werk/charles-mingus-blues-en-roots.listen: Listen to Wednesday Night Prayer Meeting and notice the churchy, soulful feeling that Mingus himself talked about.

werk/charles-mingus-east-coasting.text:
Charles Mingus recorded East Coasting in New York on 16 August 1957 and released it that autumn. The group consisted of trombonist Jimmy Knepper, trumpeter Clarence Shaw, Shafi Hadi on saxophone, drummer Dannie Richmond and pianist Bill Evans.

The record contains five original pieces by Mingus and the standard Memories of You. AllMusic calls it one of his lesser-known band sessions, but finds the music stimulating: it stretches the boundaries of bop and is never predictable. The 1993 CD reissue added extra recordings, including alternate takes.
werk/charles-mingus-east-coasting.listen: In West Coast Ghost, the longest track, listen to how the soloists take turns and to what the pianist does underneath.

werk/charles-mingus-mingus-ah-um.text:
Charles Mingus recorded this album in May 1959 for Columbia, the first he made for that label. It was released in October of that year. The title is a corrupted Latin list: Mingus, Minga, Mingum. The Penguin Guide to Jazz called the record an extended homage to ancestors, and that fits the pieces. Better Git It In Your Soul draws on gospel and preaching, Goodbye Pork Pie Hat is a tribute to Lester Young, who died shortly before the recording, and Open Letter to Duke is for Duke Ellington.

Fables of Faubus is named after Governor Orval Faubus of Arkansas, who in 1957 blocked the integration of schools in Little Rock. Columbia refused the political lyrics on the album, so the piece was released as an instrumental. The original LP also contained shortened versions of six of the nine pieces. In 2003 the album was added to the National Recording Registry of the Library of Congress.
werk/charles-mingus-mingus-ah-um.listen: In Boogie Stop Shuffle, listen to how the boogie bass carries the piece and how the music switches between stop time and shuffle.

werk/charles-mingus-pithecanthropus-erec.text:
This album was released in August 1956 on Atlantic. Charles Mingus taught his musicians the pieces by ear for the first time instead of writing them out on paper. The line-up includes alto saxophonist Jackie McLean and pianist Mal Waldron.

The title track lasts well over ten minutes. According to the liner notes it is a symphonic poem about the rise of man from his ancestors to his fall, through greed and through the failure to see that the oppressed must be freed. The title refers to Java Man, at the time the oldest known human fossil. The Penguin Guide to Jazz calls the record one of the truly great modern jazz albums and sees in the interplay of the first track a key to the free collective improvisation of the following decade.
werk/charles-mingus-pithecanthropus-erec.listen: In Pithecanthropus Erectus, listen to how the whole group plays together instead of taking solos in turn.

werk/charles-mingus-the-black-saint-and-.text:
Charles Mingus recorded this record on 20 January 1963 with a band of eleven musicians, and Impulse! released it in July of that year. The whole album is one continuous composition, partly written as a ballet and divided into four tracks and six parts. Bob Hammer was co-orchestrator and arranger. His rehearsal band worked the piece out during a six-week engagement at the Village Vanguard. Mingus wrote the liner notes together with his then psychotherapist Edmund Pollock.

Mingus himself described the orchestral style as ethnic folk-dance music. Critics hear jazz and classical music in it, with elements of African music and Spanish themes. Q described the atmosphere as a blend of twilight blues, dancing vitality and Andalusian heat. The record is regarded as one of the most acclaimed jazz albums of the twentieth century and as one of Mingus's two major works, alongside Mingus Ah Um. AllMusic calls it one of the greatest achievements in jazz orchestration.
werk/charles-mingus-the-black-saint-and-.listen: Listen to Track A, Solo Dancer, and notice how the eleven-piece band sounds like a small orchestra, with shifting colours and moods in one continuous piece.

werk/charles-mingus-the-clown.text:
The Clown was released in September 1957 on Atlantic Records. It was recorded on 13 February and 12 March of that year. Mingus said he chose these four pieces because some musicians said he did not swing. He therefore made pieces that did, and recorded a blues for the first time.

The album is best known for its title piece. In it the radio presenter Jean Shepherd tells a story about a clown who wants to please everyone and is only appreciated once he is dead. Shepherd improvised his text and changed the ending, so that the listener is left to fill in more for themselves. Mingus had the musicians overdub parts, because the piece plays in several keys at once. He wrote Reincarnation of a Lovebird for Charlie Parker. In Haitian Fight Song, according to Mingus, sorrow and determination come through.
werk/charles-mingus-the-clown.listen: Listen to The Clown and follow how the narrator Jean Shepherd tells the story of the clown, with the band around him.

werk/charli-xcx-brat.text:
Charli XCX made BRAT as her sixth album and the first after the extension of her contract with Atlantic Records in 2023. The production was handled by, among others, A. G. Cook, Finn Keane, Cirkut and her partner George Daniel. The record draws on the English rave scene of the 2000s, where she began performing as a teenager. She called it her most aggressive and confrontational work, but also her most vulnerable. The sound, in her own words, is minimalist, but very loud and brash.

Girl, so confusing is about a difficult relationship with another singer, later confirmed as Lorde, who took part in a remix. Rewind was a response to the success of Speed Drive. So I is about grief over Sophie. The critical response was exceptionally good, the album was nominated for the Mercury Prize and won three Grammys. The cover set off Brat Summer.
werk/charli-xcx-brat.listen: In Girl, so confusing, listen to the lyrics about a tense bond with another singer. Notice how the combination of hard club music and vulnerable words works.

werk/charli-xcx-true-romance.text:
True Romance is the debut album by the British singer Charli XCX and was released on 12 April 2013, a year later than planned. The groundwork was laid in 2010, when she met producer Ariel Rechtshaid in Los Angeles. In two hours they wrote Stay Away. With the Swede Patrik Berger she made You're the One. Another beat from that collaboration became I Love It, the song that made Icona Pop an international hit in 2012. Many of the songs had already appeared on the EP You're the One and on two mixtapes. The title refers to the film True Romance and, according to her, is about a raw, honest view of her love life.

The album sounds like synth-pop with dark, gothic colours. Critics were mostly positive: Pitchfork praised the mix of 1980s synth-pop, girl groups and modern producers, while NME found the record monotonous in the long run.
werk/charli-xcx-true-romance.listen: Listen to You're the One and notice the deep bass: how does it give the song a dark atmosphere while the melody stays pop?

werk/charlie-byrd-mr-guitar.text:
Mr. Guitar contains recordings that guitarist Charlie Byrd made in 1960. The album was released in 1962 on Riverside. It had previously come out as Jazz at the Showboat, Vol. 3 on the Offbeat label of Washington Records, but that release had only limited distribution, before Byrd signed with Riverside.

It is a trio record. Byrd plays guitar, Keter Betts bass and Bertell Knox drums. Alongside his own pieces such as Blues for Felix and Funky Flamenco there are songs by Duke Ellington and George and Ira Gershwin. AllMusic gave the album four and a half stars and called it a delightful trio performance with an agile, light atmosphere. It is thus a record on which the guitar does not dominate, but plays lightly and playfully with bass and drums.
werk/charlie-byrd-mr-guitar.listen: Listen to Funky Flamenco and notice how Byrd makes the guitar sound here and how bass and drums follow him.

werk/charlie-haden-as-long-as-there-s-mu.text:
As Long as There's Music is an album of duets by bassist Charlie Haden and pianist Hampton Hawes. It was recorded in 1976 and released in 1978 on Artists House. It contains original compositions by Hawes and the bassist, and music by others. This Is Called Love is a variant on Cole Porter's What Is This Thing Called Love. The 1993 CD reissue added a bonus track that had previously appeared on The Golden Number, and three alternate takes.

The sessions took place in Burbank and Los Angeles. AllMusic called the music calm and often lyrical, with many thoughtful and subtle ideas from two masters. DownBeat gave it four stars and spoke of an album full of beautiful secret knowledge.
werk/charlie-haden-as-long-as-there-s-mu.listen: Listen to Irene and notice how bass and piano answer each other like two equal voices.

werk/charlie-haden-folk-songs.text:
Folk Songs was recorded in November 1979 and released in February 1981 on ECM. Bassist Charlie Haden plays here in a trio with saxophonist Jan Garbarek and guitarist Egberto Gismonti. It was their second album together, after Magico from 1980. Garbarek plays soprano and tenor saxophone, Gismonti guitar and piano.

The album contains six pieces. Folk Song is a traditional, Bodas de Prata and Cego Aderaldo are by Gismonti, Veien is by Garbarek and For Turiya is by Haden himself. Equilibrista is also by Gismonti. Scott Yanow of AllMusic called it one of the better ECM recordings, full of sombre original pieces, improvisations in which jazz and world music come together and atmospheric interplay. According to him the record works well as background music and also when you listen to it attentively.
werk/charlie-haden-folk-songs.listen: In For Turiya, listen to Haden's bass, the piece he wrote himself, and notice how saxophone and guitar play around it.

werk/charlie-haden-liberation-music-orch.text:
This was the first album on which bassist Charlie Haden was the leader. The occasion was songs from the Spanish Civil War, three of which he put on the record, old folk songs with new words. In addition there are War Orphans by Ornette Coleman, three pieces by Carla Bley, who did much of the arranging, and two compositions by Haden himself. Song for Ché is dedicated to Che Guevara. Circus '68 '69 is about the 1968 Democratic convention, where delegations sang We Shall Overcome while the convention orchestra drowned them out with You're a Grand Old Flag.

In that piece the group is therefore split into two bands, to re-enact the events on the convention floor. The album is a politically charged piece of jazz for a large ensemble. In Rolling Stone, Lester Bangs praised above all Bley's arrangements. Robert Christgau was less enthusiastic. A sequel did not follow until 1983.
werk/charlie-haden-liberation-music-orch.listen: Listen to Circus '68 '69 and notice how two bands play at the same time and seem to work against each other, as at the 1968 convention.

werk/charlie-haden-the-golden-number.text:
The Golden Number consists of four duets by bassist Charlie Haden, recorded in 1976 and released in 1977 on Horizon. It was his second duo album for that label, after Closeness from 1976. His partners are trumpeter Don Cherry, who also plays flute, tenor saxophonist Archie Shepp, pianist Hampton Hawes and Ornette Coleman, who plays trumpet here. Hawes died shortly before its release, and the bassist dedicated the work to him in the liner notes.

The recording took place in several locations, in Burbank, Los Angeles and New York. AllMusic gave it four stars, and Scott Yanow found the music intriguing and varied. Ethan Iverson called the album essential. Of Turnaround he wrote that Hawes stayed with the bass every second and responded to those otherworldly notes with flawless choices.
werk/charlie-haden-the-golden-number.listen: Listen to Turnaround and notice how Hampton Hawes's piano responds to the bass.

werk/charlie-parker-south-of-the-border.text:
South of the Border was released in 1952 on Mercury Records as a 10-inch LP. In 1995 an expanded CD version appeared on Verve, and all the tracks are also on the Verve box set Bird: The Complete Charlie Parker on Verve. Here the saxophonist plays in a Latin American setting, with, among others, Machito and his orchestra.

According to AllMusic his improvisational style barely changed. He played his lightning-fast bop phrases over congas and bongos, and they fitted the grooves almost effortlessly. He did, however, adapt his phrasing of the melodies to the rhythms. The Penguin Guide to Jazz thought it was time to put an end to the snobbery surrounding these fine records and gave the original album three of its four stars.
werk/charlie-parker-south-of-the-border.listen: Listen to Mango Mangue and notice how the saxophone keeps playing above the congas and bongos.

werk/chavela-vargas-noche-bohemia.text:
Noche Bohemia was the debut of the Mexican singer Chavela Vargas. It was released in 1961 on the Orfeón label, and on the sleeve her name appears as Chabela Vargas. It was the first of more than eighty records she would make.

On the recordings the guitarist Antonio Bribiesca accompanies her, so that the sound remains very sparse: mostly voice and guitar can be heard. The record has twelve songs, six on each side, including pieces by Agustín Lara and José Alfredo Jiménez. The song Macorina later became one of her best-known numbers. The record thus marks the beginning of a long recording career, which would comprise more than eighty albums in total.
werk/chavela-vargas-noche-bohemia.listen: In Macorina, listen to how Chavela Vargas's voice and Antonio Bribiesca's guitar together carry the song.

werk/cheap-trick-heaven-tonight.text:
Heaven Tonight is Cheap Trick's third studio album. Producer Tom Werman recorded it and it was released on 24 April 1978. The debut showed the band's dark, raw side and In Color a lighter, more pop-oriented side. On this album the two come together: a rock record full of hooks with a good dose of cheek.

Among the best-known songs are Surrender, Auf Wiedersehen, the title track and a cover of California Man by The Move. The album is said to be the first ever recorded with a twelve-string electric bass. There is a story about the sleeve: the record company wanted to call the record American Standard, a wink at the manufacturer of bathroom fixtures. The band thought nothing of it, but did keep the photograph, which shows the four of them standing in a public toilet. Many fans and critics see Heaven Tonight as the group's best album.
werk/cheap-trick-heaven-tonight.listen: Listen to Oh Claire, a jam of about a minute in which only the words Oh, konnichi wa are sung. Hear how briefly and amusingly the band closes the album.

werk/cheap-trick-in-color.text:
In Color is Cheap Trick's second studio album, released in 1977 and produced by Tom Werman. Unlike on the debut, the production sounds smoother, in the hope of a commercial breakthrough. The band was deeply dissatisfied. Bassist Tom Petersson later said that the label wanted to make them sound radio-friendly and safe, which meant losing their own sound. In the United States the record did only moderately, but in Japan I Want You to Want Me and Clock Strikes Ten became hits.

Five of the ten tracks later appeared in live versions on Cheap Trick at Budokan. There I Want You to Want Me became a US Top 10 hit, and it is still the group's best-known song. The album is regarded as a power pop classic. In 2003 Rolling Stone placed it at number 443 on its list of the 500 greatest albums.
werk/cheap-trick-in-color.listen: Listen to I Want You to Want Me and notice how polished the studio version sounds. Then compare it with the live version on Cheap Trick at Budokan.

werk/cher-all-i-really-want-to-do.text:
All I Really Want to Do was released on 16 August 1965 on Imperial Records and was Cher's first solo album, while she was also having success at Atco as one half of the duo Sonny & Cher. After the hit I Got You Babe, Bono decided to launch his wife as a solo artist too. He produced the record, Harold Battiste wrote the arrangements and the sessions ended in June 1965 at Gold Star Studios in Hollywood.

It is largely a covers album with a folky edge, to set it apart from the duo's records. It includes three songs by Bob Dylan, Needles and Pins, which Bono co-wrote, and I Go to Sleep by Ray Davies. The title song was the only single. The idea came from the Byrds, whom she saw perform at Ciro's on the Sunset Strip, and the two versions competed for chart positions. According to AllMusic she sounds young and full of life.
werk/cher-all-i-really-want-to-do.listen: Listen to All I Really Want to Do and notice how the vocal is set in a folk-rock arrangement, with guitars and an almost Spector-like rich backdrop.

werk/cher-the-sonny-side-of-cher.text:
The Sonny Side of Chér was released on 28 March 1966, shortly after the success of Cher's debut album. She recorded it while she was also in the charts as one half of Sonny & Cher. Sonny Bono produced the record. He kept to the formula of the first album: newly arranged covers, supplemented with new songs from his own hand.

The track list draws on folk and pop, with influences from French chanson. It includes Like a Rolling Stone by Bob Dylan, It's Not Unusual, The Girl From Ipanema and Milord by Edith Piaf. According to the source, Ol' Man River already shows how powerful her voice was. Bang Bang (My Baby Shot Me Down), written by Bono, became her first solo hit in the US top ten. Where Do You Go was the first single. The critical response was mixed: Billboard found the record well produced, while AllMusic called it formulaic.
werk/cher-the-sonny-side-of-cher.listen: Listen to Bang Bang (My Baby Shot Me Down) and notice how Cher sings the story of the song: does she keep her voice restrained or does she add force?

werk/chet-baker-chet-baker-sings.text:
Chet Baker Sings is the trumpeter's first vocal album, released in 1954 by Pacific Jazz Records. Until then he had been almost exclusively an instrumentalist. His mother had been asking him for years to sing more, and in October 1953 he had already sung on two tracks. After that he wanted to record a whole record of vocals, to the scepticism of producer Dick Bock. It was recorded in Hollywood and pianist Russ Freeman chose a number of the songs. According to biographer James Gavin, Bock was worried, because Baker had trouble singing in tune and many takes of each song were needed.

Reactions were sharply divided. Critics called his voice soft and effeminate, which clashed with the masculine image of jazz singers at the time. Even so the record grew into a great success, especially with women. In the year of its release DownBeat voted him best trumpeter and best vocalist. The album received a Grammy Hall of Fame Award in 2001 and also inspired bossa nova.
werk/chet-baker-chet-baker-sings.listen: In My Funny Valentine, listen to the soft, vulnerable singing voice and the small accompanying group: how little it takes to carry the song.

werk/chet-baker-the-trumpet-artistry-of-.text:
The Trumpet Artistry of Chet Baker is a compilation on the Pacific Jazz label with recordings from 1953 and 1954, made in Los Angeles and Hollywood. The album contains tracks that had previously appeared on the ten-inch LP Chet Baker Sextet, supplemented with material that had not yet been released. The line-up varies from session to session. Pianist Russ Freeman plays on it, on some tracks we hear Bob Brookmeyer on valve trombone and on others the saxophonists Herb Geller, Jack Montrose, Bob Gordon and Bud Shank. Freeman himself wrote, among others, No Ties, Happy Little Sunbeam and Bea's Flat.

The programme consists largely of standards by composers such as Jerome Kern and Jimmy Van Heusen, such as All the Things You Are and Imagination, supplemented with Goodbye by Gordon Jenkins. AllMusic gave the record three stars and called it a perfect introduction to the trumpeter's early music.
werk/chet-baker-the-trumpet-artistry-of-.listen: In I'm Glad There Is You, listen to the interplay of trumpet and valve trombone.

werk/chic-c-est-chic.text:
C'est Chic was Chic's second studio album and was released in 1978 on Atlantic Records. All the songs were written by Bernard Edwards and Nile Rodgers. The album contains Le Freak, the group's big hit, which in October 1978 topped the US Hot 100, the R&B chart and the club chart. I Want Your Love was also a success.

It was the band's most commercially successful album and spent eleven weeks at the top of the US R&B chart. Billboard named it the R&B album of 1979. In Europe it first came out as Très Chic, with a daring sleeve and a different track list. That version was withdrawn and replaced by C'est Chic with a less risqué sleeve. The critical response was mixed: one paper spoke of a stylish take on disco, another found little of note apart from Le Freak.
werk/chic-c-est-chic.listen: Listen to Le Freak and notice how the chorus and the rhythm section stay in a tight, repeating pattern from start to finish.

werk/chic-real-people.text:
Real People is Chic's fourth album and was released in 1980 on Atlantic Records. Bernard Edwards and Nile Rodgers wrote and produced it in a year in which they were also working on records by Sister Sledge, Sheila and B. Devotion and Diana Ross. It was recorded at The Power Station in New York. The singles were Rebels Are We and Real People, and in the United Kingdom only, also 26.

The album did modestly commercially compared with Diana Ross's work and with earlier Chic records, probably because of the anti-disco backlash. Robert Christgau called it better than Risqué and praised the bouncy rhythms and Rodgers's sharp guitar. He placed it at number fifteen on his 1980 year-end list. AllMusic later found it a fine but not essential record, with Rebels Are We, I Got Protection and Chip Off the Old Block as highlights.
werk/chic-real-people.listen: Listen to Rebels Are We and notice the guitar and the bass guitar: how do those two lock together to keep the rhythm going?

werk/chic-risque.text:
Risqué is Chic's third studio album and was released in July 1979 on Atlantic. Producers Bernard Edwards and Nile Rodgers recorded everything at The Power Station in New York, with additional work at Electric Lady Studios. The album contains three hits: Good Times, My Forbidden Lover and My Feet Keep Dancing. Good Times reached number one on the US pop and R&B charts. In My Feet Keep Dancing, tap dancers tap along.

Reviewers praised the lyrics and the tone. The beat sounded firmer and the vocals were arranged to demand attention. A BBC reviewer called the album Chic's most sustained artistic statement, a celebration of a 1970s that collapsed under its own excess. Risqué also influenced hip hop, art rock and new wave. Good Times was widely sampled, most famously in Rapper's Delight by The Sugarhill Gang, the first rap single in the top 40.
werk/chic-risque.listen: In Good Times, listen to the interplay of the bass line and the rhythm guitar. Notice how they give each other space.

werk/chick-corea-a-r-c.text:
A.R.C. was recorded from 11 to 13 January 1971 by Chick Corea with bassist Dave Holland and drummer Barry Altschul. The trio had shortly before recorded The Song of Singing together. The album was released that same year on ECM, and it was the first project in Holland's long association with that label. The title stands for affinity, reality, communication, a concept from Scientology, with which the pianist was involved at the time.

The same three musicians were then also playing together in Circle, the avant-garde quartet with Anthony Braxton. According to Scott Yanow's review on AllMusic, the music on this album is less free than that of Circle, but often exploratory. He calls it a good set of adventurous jazz, recorded a few months before the pianist chose a different direction.
werk/chick-corea-a-r-c.listen: In A.R.C., listen to how piano, bass and drums talk to each other. Notice who takes the lead at any given moment.

werk/chick-corea-now-he-sings-now-he-sob.text:
This second studio album by Chick Corea was released in December 1968 on Solid State Records. Corea plays in a trio with bassist Miroslav Vitouš and drummer Roy Haynes. All the pieces are improvisations on Corea's ideas, a few of them completely free, such as The Law of Falling and Catching Up. The title comes from the I Ching, a passage about the whole range of human experiences and emotions.

On release DownBeat gave the record zero stars, because the reviewer did not know what to make of it. Later the album grew into a piano trio classic. AllMusic sees in it the start of Corea's adventurous career, and the title track received a Grammy Hall of Fame Award in 1999.
werk/chick-corea-now-he-sings-now-he-sob.listen: Listen to Now He Sings, Now He Sobs and notice how bass and drums follow and challenge the piano, as if they were three equal voices.

werk/chick-corea-the-song-of-singing.text:
The sessions took place in April 1970 and lasted two days. Blue Note released the album the following year. It is a trio session with Chick Corea on piano, Dave Holland on bass and Barry Altschul on drums. Together those three made up three quarters of Circle, an ensemble that played free jazz. Only Anthony Braxton is missing here.

On the same day, 7 April 1970, Miles Davis recorded the album Jack Johnson without the pianist. The 1987 CD reissue added two extra tracks, which had already appeared in the 1970s on Circling In and Circulus. In 1989 the last unreleased track from the sessions was added.
werk/chick-corea-the-song-of-singing.listen: Listen to Nefertitti and notice how piano, bass and drums play with each other in this small line-up.

werk/chick-corea-tones-for-joan-s-bones.text:
This debut album by Chick Corea was recorded in 1966 and released in April 1968 on Vortex Records, a subsidiary of Atlantic. The quintet features saxophonist Joe Farrell, trumpeter Woody Shaw, bassist Steve Swallow and drummer Joe Chambers. Herbie Mann produced. Corea had already recorded with, among others, Mongo Santamaria and Cal Tjader, so he was no beginner.

Litha was later recorded by Stan Getz, and Blue Mitchell had recorded Tones for Joan's Bones and Straight Up and Down shortly before. DownBeat gave the record 4.5 stars and called it a real sleeper. AllMusic speaks of a solid, sophisticated hard bop record. The Penguin Guide calls the title piece a jazz classic.
werk/chick-corea-tones-for-joan-s-bones.listen: Listen to Litha, the opening track, and notice how the horns and the rhythm section together create a brisk hard bop atmosphere.

werk/chico-hamilton-drumfusion.text:
Drumfusion is an album by drummer and bandleader Chico Hamilton, recorded in 1962 and released on Columbia. All the compositions are by Charles Lloyd, who plays tenor saxophone and flute in the band. Trombonist Garnett Brown, guitarist Gábor Szabó and bassist Albert Stinson also play. The line-up is unusual: alongside saxophone and flute we hear trombone and guitar, while the bandleader himself sits behind the drums. The six pieces last between five and well over eight minutes.

AllMusic reviewer Scott Yanow finds the music at moments melodic, but not boppish, and in places free, but not avant-garde. According to him it is a consistently infectious and inspiring band.
werk/chico-hamilton-drumfusion.listen: Listen to One for Joan and try to hear which instruments carry the melody and who solos afterwards.

werk/chico-hamilton-man-from-two-worlds.text:
Man from Two Worlds was recorded in 1963 for the Impulse! label. Chico Hamilton's group of 1962 and 1963, a quartet or quintet, is regarded by critic Scott Yanow as one of the best he had. The album received little attention at the time. The band featured Charles Lloyd on tenor saxophone and flute, Gábor Szabó on guitar and Albert Stinson on bass. Charles Lloyd wrote almost all the pieces.

According to Yanow, the group put more emphasis on melody and softer sounds than the avant-garde bands of the time, but still pushed at the boundaries of the music. He gave the album four and a half stars. The CD reissue has four extra tracks from the previous record, Passin' Thru. The longest track on the original album is Forest Flower, which lasts well over ten minutes.
werk/chico-hamilton-man-from-two-worlds.listen: Listen to Forest Flower, the longest piece on the record, and notice how melody and soft sounds take centre stage here.

werk/childish-gambino-awaken-my-love.text:
Donald Glover released this third album under the name Childish Gambino on 2 December 2016 on Glassnote Records. He produced it with Ludwig Göransson. It was his first step away from hip hop, towards psychedelic soul, funk and R&B. In June 2016 he announced it with the app pharos.earth, and in September he played the album over three nights in Joshua Tree, where he performed eleven songs in a funk and jazz style, with hardly any rapping.

The sleeve refers to Funkadelic's Maggot Brain from 1971. Critics heard the funkadelia of the 1970s in an ambitious, emotional album. Me and Your Mama was the first single, and Redbone followed a week later. The album received Grammy nominations for Album of the Year and Best Urban Contemporary Album, and Redbone won the Grammy for Best Traditional R&B Performance.
werk/childish-gambino-awaken-my-love.listen: Listen to Redbone and notice the falsetto vocals and the sound of the bass and the rhythm section.

werk/chris-thile-leading-off.text:
Chris Thile was thirteen when his first solo album was released on 25 September 1994 on Sugar Hill Records. He is counted among the newgrass musicians and plays mandolin, but on this album also fiddle and guitar, and he made the arrangements himself. Scott Thile plays bass, Sean Watkins mandolin, and guests such as fiddler Byron Berline, banjo player Dennis Caplinger and fiddler Stuart Duncan join in. Pete Wernick, also a banjo player, produced.

Well over half of the thirteen tracks are by Thile himself, sometimes together with Watkins. In addition there are Panhandle Rag by Leon McAuliffe, Old Dangerfield by Bill Monroe, the traditional Salt Creek, a medley of old favourites and the hymn How Great Thou Art.
werk/chris-thile-leading-off.listen: Listen to Salt Creek and remember, with every note of the mandolin, that the player was only thirteen.
